nodes.title: Colors
nodes.goal: Name colors and mix them.

lesson_media.alt: Equal dabs of classroom blue and yellow paint are shown before mixing and as an approximate green mixture, with separate brushes and a clean palette.
lesson_media.caption: Equal parts of these classroom blue and yellow paints make an approximate green. Real pigment mixtures vary; screens add colored light instead and follow different mixing rules.

lesson_media.title: Mix two classroom paints
lesson_media.instructions: Choose two classroom paint colors and combine equal parts. Compare the model's approximate recipe with the two starting swatches; real paints can mix differently.

nodes.kid_text: In many classrooms, red, yellow and blue paints are a handy set for learning to mix colors. Equal parts of classroom blue and yellow often look green, but real results depend on the pigments and amounts. Red, yellow and blue are one teaching model, not the only possible set of primaries. Phone and television screens mix red, green and blue light instead, so their recipes are different.

quiz.prompt: Which one is red? 🍎🍌🫐
quiz.say: Which one of these is red? Is it the apple, the banana, or the blueberry?
quiz.explain: Yes, the shiny apple is red!

quiz.prompt: Mix equal parts classroom blue 🔵 and yellow 🟡 paint. About what color?
choices: Green
Purple
Black
quiz.answer: Green
quiz.say: If you swirl equal parts classroom blue and yellow paint together, about what color do you get? Green, purple, or black?
quiz.explain: These classroom blue and yellow paints make an approximate green. The exact result depends on the pigments and amounts.

quiz.prompt: Mix equal parts classroom red 🔴 and yellow 🟡 paint. About what color?
choices: Orange
Purple
Green
quiz.answer: Orange
quiz.say: Now swirl equal parts classroom red and yellow paint together. About what color appears? Orange, purple, or green?
quiz.explain: These classroom red and yellow paints make an approximate orange. Different pigments can shift the result.

quiz.prompt: Which one is yellow? 🍋🍇🍓
quiz.say: Which one of these is yellow? The grapes, the lemon, or the strawberry?
quiz.explain: The lemon is bright yellow, just like the sun!

quiz.prompt: Mix equal parts classroom red 🔴 and blue 🔵 paint. About what color?
choices: Purple
Brown
Green
quiz.answer: Purple
quiz.say: If you swirl equal parts classroom red and blue paint together, about what color do you get? Purple, brown, or green?
quiz.explain: These classroom red and blue paints make an approximate purple. The pigments used can make it brighter or duller.

quiz.prompt: Do screen lights mix just like classroom paints?
choices: No — screens add colored light
Yes — both use the same recipes
quiz.answer: No — screens add colored light
quiz.say: Do screen lights mix just like classroom paints? No, screens add colored light, or yes, both use the same recipes?
quiz.explain: No. Screens usually add red, green and blue light, while paints contain pigments that absorb some light. Their mixing recipes are different.

quiz.prompt: Mix equal parts classroom white ⚪ and red 🔴 paint. About what color?
choices: Pink
Purple
Orange
quiz.answer: Pink
quiz.say: Now stir equal parts classroom white and red paint. About what color do you get? Pink, purple, or orange?
quiz.explain: These classroom white and red paints make an approximate pink. More white would usually make the mixture lighter.

nodes.title: Drawing and Painting
nodes.goal: Make marks; draw what you see and imagine.
nodes.kid_text: A drawing starts with just one little mark from your crayon, and every mark you add tells more of the story. Look at your teddy bear and make a round line for its head and two little lines for its ears. You can draw things you see, and you can draw things you only imagine, like a purple dog that flies!

quiz.prompt: Which one colors your paper? 🖍️ 🕯️ 🌡️
quiz.say: One of these colors your paper. Is it the crayon, the candle, or the thermometer?
quiz.explain: The crayon is the one that colors your paper!

quiz.prompt: Which line looks like a snake moving? 〰️ ➖ ⚡
quiz.say: One of these lines moves along like a snake. Is it the wiggly line, the straight line, or the zigzag line?
quiz.explain: A wiggly line waves up and down, like a little snake!

quiz.prompt: Which one is pretend? 🐎 🦄 🐕
quiz.say: Two of these you can see outside, and one lives only in your imagination. Is the pretend one the horse, the unicorn, or the dog?
quiz.explain: Unicorns live in our imagination, and we can still draw them!

quiz.prompt: Which one has soft hairs at its tip? 🖌️ ✏️ 🖍️
quiz.say: One of these has soft hairs at its tip. Is it the paintbrush, the pencil, or the crayon?
quiz.explain: A paintbrush spreads lovely wet paint across your paper!

quiz.prompt: Which line looks like the edge of a ruler? ➖ 〰️ ⚡
quiz.say: One of these lines looks like the edge of a ruler. Is it the straight line, the wiggly line, or the zigzag line?
quiz.explain: A straight line goes right across with no wiggles at all!

quiz.prompt: Which one is real? 🦎 🐉 🧜
quiz.say: One of these you could really meet, and two live only in stories. Is the real one the lizard, the dragon, or the mermaid?
quiz.explain: Lizards are real. Dragons and mermaids live in stories!

quiz.prompt: Which line zigzags? ➖ 〰️ ⚡
quiz.say: Which line goes zig, zag, zig, with sharp pointy corners? The straight one, the wiggly one, or the lightning one?
quiz.explain: A zigzag line turns sharp corners, just like lightning!

nodes.title: Songs and Sounds
nodes.goal: Sing, clap a beat, and listen.
nodes.kid_text: Singing is like talking with a tune, going up high like a little bird and down low like a big bear. When a song plays, clap your hands along with it, clap, clap, clap, and you are keeping the beat. Then stop and just listen carefully, and see if you can hear who is singing high and who is singing low.

quiz.prompt: A little bird sings 🐦. What sound?
choices: High
Low
Rumbly
quiz.answer: High
quiz.say: A little bird goes tweet, tweet, tweet. Is that sound high, low, or rumbly?
quiz.explain: Little birds sing way up high!

quiz.prompt: Which sounds low? 🐻 🐭 🐤
quiz.say: Which one makes a low, deep, rumbly sound? The big bear, the little mouse, or the baby chick?
quiz.explain: The big bear rumbles low. The mouse and the chick are high and squeaky.

quiz.prompt: How many claps? 👏👏👏
quiz.say: Listen and count with me: clap, clap, clap. How many claps was that? Was it 2, 3, or 4?
quiz.explain: That was three claps, one for each beat!

quiz.prompt: How many claps? 👏👏
quiz.say: Listen and count with me: clap, clap. How many claps was that? Was it 3, 2, or 4?
quiz.explain: That was two claps, one for each beat!

quiz.prompt: Which sounds high? 🐤 🐘 🐮
quiz.say: Which one makes a high, tiny sound? The baby chick, the big elephant, or the cow?
quiz.explain: The little chick peeps way up high. The elephant and the cow are low.

quiz.prompt: Sing like a sleeping baby is near 👶
choices: Soft
Loud
Fast
quiz.answer: Soft
quiz.say: A baby is sleeping, so you sing very, very quietly. Is your singing soft, loud, or fast?
quiz.explain: Quiet singing is soft. Big singing is loud.

quiz.prompt: Singing is talking with a…?
choices: Tune
Shout
Whisper
quiz.answer: Tune
quiz.say: Singing is like talking, but with something special added. Is it a tune, a shout, or a whisper?
quiz.explain: Singing is talking with a tune that goes up and down!

nodes.title: Moving to Music
nodes.goal: Feel rhythm through movement.
nodes.kid_text: Music has a steady heartbeat called rhythm, and your body can move right along with it. When a drum goes boom, boom, boom, stomp your feet on each boom. Fast music makes you spin and hop quickly, and slow music makes you sway gently like a tree in the wind.

quiz.prompt: The drum goes bang-bang-bang-bang! 🥁 What do you do?
choices: Hop quickly
Sway slowly
Stand still
quiz.answer: Hop quickly
quiz.say: The drum is going bang, bang, bang, bang, very quick! Do you hop quickly, sway slowly, or stand still?
quiz.explain: A quick drum makes your body move quickly — hop, hop, hop!

quiz.prompt: Slow music 🎶. How do you move?
choices: Sway slowly
Run about
Jump high
quiz.answer: Sway slowly
quiz.say: Now the music is slow and gentle. Do you sway slowly, run about, or jump high?
quiz.explain: Slow music makes you sway gently, like a tree in the wind.

quiz.prompt: Drum goes boom! 🥁 Stomp with what?
choices: Feet 👣
Hands 👐
Knees 🦵
quiz.answer: Feet 👣
quiz.say: When the drum goes boom, boom, boom, what do you stomp with? Your feet, your hands, or your knees?
quiz.explain: You stomp with your feet. Hands clap and knees bend, but feet stomp!

quiz.prompt: Music stops! 🔇 What do you do?
choices: Freeze
Spin
Clap
quiz.answer: Freeze
quiz.say: Uh oh, the music stopped! Do you freeze, spin, or clap?
quiz.explain: When the music stops, your body stops too!

quiz.prompt: Which moves fast? 🐢 🐇 🐌
quiz.say: Which one moves fast, like fast music? Is it the turtle, the rabbit, or the snail?
quiz.explain: The rabbit hops fast, just like fast music!

quiz.prompt: Music's steady heartbeat is called…?
choices: Rhythm
Melody
Words
quiz.answer: Rhythm
quiz.say: Music has a steady heartbeat that your body can move to. Is it called the rhythm, the melody, or the words?
quiz.explain: Rhythm is the steady heartbeat of the music. The melody is the tune that goes up and down, and the words are what you sing!

quiz.prompt: Fast drums! 🥁 How do you move?
choices: Run
Tiptoe
Sit down
quiz.answer: Run
quiz.say: The drums are going fast and loud! Do you run, tiptoe, or sit down?
quiz.explain: Fast drums make your body move fast, run, run, run!

nodes.title: Elements of Art
nodes.goal: Line, shape, color, texture and pattern.
nodes.kid_text: Every picture is built from a few simple building blocks, just like a house is built from bricks. A line can be straight, wiggly, or zigzag, and when lines join up they make a shape, like a circle or a square. Texture is how something would feel, bumpy tree bark or soft fur, and a pattern is when shapes or colors repeat, like the stripes on a bee.

quiz.prompt: What comes next? 🔴🔵🔴🔵…
quiz.say: Look at this pattern: red, blue, red, blue. What comes next? Red, blue, or yellow?
quiz.explain: A pattern repeats itself, so red comes next!

quiz.prompt: Which one feels soft? 🐑 🪨 🧱
quiz.say: Which one feels soft when you touch it? Is it the sheep, the rock, or the brick?
quiz.explain: How something feels, soft or bumpy, is called texture.

quiz.prompt: Which one is a shape? ⬜ 〰️ ➖
quiz.say: One of these is a shape and two are just lines. Is it the white box, the wavy one, or the flat one?
quiz.explain: When lines join all the way around, they make a shape, like a square!

quiz.prompt: What comes next? 🟩🟩🟥🟩🟩🟥…
quiz.say: Look at this pattern: green, green, red, green, green, red. What comes next? Red, green, or yellow?
quiz.explain: The pattern keeps repeating, so green comes next!

quiz.prompt: Which feels rough? 🧱 🎈 🐑
quiz.say: Which one feels rough and scratchy when you touch it? The brick, the balloon, or the sheep?
quiz.explain: The brick feels rough, and rough is a kind of texture!

quiz.prompt: Zigzag and curvy are kinds of…?
choices: Lines
Shapes
Colors
quiz.answer: Lines
quiz.say: Zigzag, curvy, and straight are all kinds of what? Lines, shapes, or colors?
quiz.explain: Lines can zigzag, curve, or go straight across your page!

quiz.prompt: Dark gray storm clouds ⛈. How does it feel?
choices: Gloomy
Cheerful
Silly
quiz.answer: Gloomy
quiz.say: A picture full of dark gray storm clouds. How does it make you feel? Gloomy, cheerful, or silly?
quiz.explain: Dark colors can feel gloomy, and bright colors can feel cheerful.

nodes.title: Making Things
nodes.goal: Sculpture, collage and craft.
nodes.kid_text: You can make art you can pick up and hold in your hands! Squish and pinch clay into a bumpy little dinosaur, and now you have a sculpture, art you can walk all the way around. Or tear up colored paper and glue the pieces onto a page to make a collage, sticking many small bits into one big picture.

quiz.prompt: You squish clay into a dino 🦕. That is a…
choices: Sculpture
Collage
Painting
quiz.answer: Sculpture
quiz.say: You squish and pinch clay into a little dinosaur you can hold. Is that a sculpture, a collage, or a painting?
quiz.explain: Art you can hold and walk around is called a sculpture!

quiz.prompt: Torn paper glued on a page 📄. That is a…
choices: Collage
Sculpture
Painting
quiz.answer: Collage
quiz.say: You tear up colored paper and glue the little pieces onto a page. Is that a collage, a sculpture, or a painting?
quiz.explain: Many small bits glued into one big picture is a collage!

quiz.prompt: Which can you walk around? 🗿 🖼️ 📄
quiz.say: Which artwork can you walk all the way around? The statue, the picture on the wall, or the sheet of paper?
quiz.explain: A statue is a sculpture, so you can see every single side!

quiz.prompt: You roll snow into a snowman ⛄. It is a…
choices: Sculpture
Collage
Painting
quiz.answer: Sculpture
quiz.say: You roll snow into a snowman you can walk all the way around. Is it a sculpture, a collage, or a painting?
quiz.explain: A snowman is a sculpture made out of snow!

quiz.prompt: Which one is flat? 🖼️ 🗿 ⛄
quiz.say: Which artwork is flat against the wall? The picture, the statue, or the snowman?
quiz.explain: A picture is flat. Statues and snowmen have sides all the way around!

quiz.prompt: Paint brushed onto paper in swirls 🎨. That is a…
choices: Collage
Sculpture
Painting
quiz.answer: Painting
quiz.say: Someone brushes paint onto paper in swirls. Is that a collage, a sculpture, or a painting?
quiz.explain: Colour brushed onto a surface makes a painting.

quiz.prompt: Which can you squish and shape?
choices: Clay
Paint
Paper
quiz.answer: Clay
quiz.say: Which one can you squish and pinch into a shape with your hands? Clay, paint, or paper?
quiz.explain: Clay squishes into any shape your hands want to make!

nodes.title: Musical Instruments
nodes.goal: Families of instruments and how they sound.
nodes.kid_text: Instruments belong to families, and each family makes its sound in its own way. You hit or shake a drum to make a boom or a rattle, so drums are the percussion family. You pluck a guitar's strings or pull a bow across a violin to make them sing, so those are the string family. Listen closely to a sound and guess: was it hit, plucked, or blown?

quiz.prompt: A drum 🥁. How do you play it?
choices: Hit
Pluck
Blow
quiz.answer: Hit
quiz.say: How do you play a drum? Do you hit it, pluck it, or blow it?
quiz.explain: You hit or shake a drum, so drums are the percussion family!

quiz.prompt: A guitar 🎸. How do you play it?
choices: Pluck
Blow
Hit
quiz.answer: Pluck
quiz.say: How do you play a guitar? Do you pluck it, blow it, or hit it?
quiz.explain: You pluck the strings, so a guitar is in the string family!

quiz.prompt: Which one has strings? 🎻 🎺 🥁
quiz.say: Which instrument has strings you pull a bow across? The violin, the trumpet, or the drum?
quiz.explain: The violin has strings. You blow a trumpet and you hit a drum.

quiz.prompt: A flute 🪈. How do you play it?
choices: Blow
Hit
Pluck
quiz.answer: Blow
quiz.say: How do you play a flute? Do you blow it, hit it, or pluck it?
quiz.explain: You blow air into a flute to make it sing!

quiz.prompt: Which one do you shake? 🎹 🪇 🎻
quiz.say: Which one do you shake to make a rattly sound? The piano, the maraca, or the violin?
quiz.explain: You shake a maraca, so it joins the percussion family!

quiz.prompt: Which one needs your breath? 🎻 🎺 🪇
quiz.say: Which instrument needs your breath to make a sound? The violin, the trumpet, or the maraca?
quiz.explain: You blow air into a trumpet. You bow a violin and you shake a maraca.

quiz.prompt: Which has keys you press? 🎹 🥁 🎸
quiz.say: Which instrument has keys you press with your fingers? The piano, the drum, or the guitar?
quiz.explain: A piano has keys to press, a drum you hit, and a guitar you pluck!

nodes.title: Beat and Melody
nodes.goal: Keep a beat; follow a tune.
nodes.kid_text: A beat is the steady tick-tock that stays the same the whole way through a song, like feet marching in a line. The melody is the tune that dances up and down on top of the beat, and it is the part you hum after the song ends. Try tapping the steady beat with your foot while your voice follows the melody at the same time.

quiz.prompt: How does a beat go? 🥁
choices: Steady
Wobbly
Faster and faster
quiz.answer: Steady
quiz.say: A beat is like feet marching in a line. Does it go steady, wobbly, or faster and faster?
quiz.explain: The beat stays steady, tick-tock, the whole way through a song!

quiz.prompt: Which part do you hum? 🎵
choices: Melody
Beat
Drum
quiz.answer: Melody
quiz.say: After a song is over, which part do you hum? The melody, the beat, or the drum?
quiz.explain: The melody is the tune that dances up and down, and that's what you hum!

quiz.prompt: How many taps? 👏👏👏👏
quiz.say: Listen and count the steady beat: tap, tap, tap, tap. How many taps? Was it 3, 4, or 5?
quiz.explain: Four steady taps, and that is keeping the beat!

quiz.prompt: Count the beats: 👏👏👏👏👏👏
quiz.say: Count the steady beat with me: tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap. How many was that? Was it 6, 4, or 7?
quiz.explain: Six steady taps, all exactly the same, that is the beat!

quiz.prompt: Which part stays the same all song?
choices: Beat
Melody
Words
quiz.answer: Beat
quiz.say: Which part of a song stays steady the whole way through? The beat, the melody, or the words?
quiz.explain: The beat stays steady while the melody and the words change on top!

quiz.prompt: Happy Birthday's tune 🎂 is its…?
choices: Melody
Beat
Rest
quiz.answer: Melody
quiz.say: When you sing Happy Birthday, the tune that goes up and down is called what? The melody, the beat, or a rest?
quiz.explain: The tune your voice follows is the melody!

quiz.prompt: A sleepy lullaby 🌙. What kind of beat?
choices: Slow
Fast
Loud and thumping
quiz.answer: Slow
quiz.say: A sleepy lullaby rocks you gently. Is its beat slow, fast, or loud and thumping?
quiz.explain: Lullabies have a slow, gentle beat for sleepy time!

nodes.title: Art Through Time
nodes.goal: Cave paintings to modern art.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the oldest kind of art, made by people tens of thousands of years ago?
quiz.answer: Cave paintings on rock walls
quiz.explain: The earliest known art includes prehistoric cave paintings, while oil painting, steel sculpture, and photography came many thousands of years later.
choices: Sculptures welded from steel
Cave paintings on rock walls
Color photographs of cities
Oil portraits of noble kings

quiz.prompt: Modern art often broke away from copying the world exactly. Which artwork best fits the spirit of modern art?
quiz.answer: A canvas of bold geometric shapes, not a real scene
quiz.explain: Modern art frequently moved away from lifelike representation toward abstraction and experiment, unlike traditional realistic portraits or statues.
choices: A precise, detailed map of a real city's streets
A marble statue copying the body of a real athlete
A carefully realistic portrait of a king in his robes
A canvas of bold geometric shapes, not a real scene

quiz.prompt: The painted horses in the Lascaux caves in France are about 17,000 years old. The Mona Lisa was painted about 500 years ago. How many times older are the cave horses?
quiz.explain: 17,000 divided by 500 is 34. Almost all of art's story happened before anyone built a museum to keep it in.

quiz.prompt: Cave painters had no shop to buy paint from. Where did the reds, yellows and blacks on the cave walls come from?
quiz.answer: They ground up coloured earth and soft rock, such as red and yellow ochre, and used black charcoal from the fire, mixing the powder with water or fat.
quiz.explain: Ochre is an iron-rich earth that grinds into red and yellow powder; charcoal from a burnt stick gives black. Both were underfoot, which is why the same colours turn up in caves thousands of miles apart.

quiz.prompt: A gallery hangs four pictures: a bison drawn on rock in charcoal and red earth; an Egyptian tomb wall of flat figures in profile; an oil portrait of a merchant in his study; a canvas of coloured squares showing no object at all. Which list puts them in the order they were made, oldest first?
quiz.answer: Bison, tomb wall, merchant, squares
choices: Bison, tomb wall, merchant, squares
Tomb wall, bison, merchant, then squares
Bison, tomb wall, squares, then the merchant
Squares, merchant, tomb wall, bison
quiz.explain: Cave painting comes first by tens of thousands of years, then Egypt, then the oil portraits of the last few hundred years, then abstract painting, which is barely a century old. Simple-looking does not mean old.

quiz.prompt: In Egyptian tomb paintings the tomb's owner is drawn far bigger than the servants standing beside him, even though they share the same patch of floor. What is the painter telling us?
quiz.answer: Who matters most in rank, not who stands closest
choices: Who matters most in rank, not who stands closest
That the servants were standing much further away
That the painter had not learned to draw people the same size
That the owner really did tower over everyone in his household
quiz.explain: Egyptian painters used size for rank, not for distance: the bigger the figure, the more important the person. Drawing size to show distance came much later.

quiz.prompt: A museum labels a marble statue 'about 2,450 years old' and a mosaic floor 'about 1,900 years old'. Which was made first, and how can you tell?
quiz.answer: The statue, because a bigger age means longer ago
choices: The statue, because a bigger age means longer ago
The mosaic, because 1,900 is the smaller number
The statue, because marble lasts longer than tile does
Neither, since both were made in ancient times
quiz.explain: An age counts backwards from today, so the larger number is the older object.

quiz.prompt: A tomb painting is about 4,500 years old. A century is 100 years. About how many centuries old is it?
quiz.explain: 4,500 divided by 100 gives 45 centuries.

quiz.prompt: Before cameras existed, wealthy families paid painters for portraits. Which job did photographs later take over from those paintings?
quiz.answer: Keeping a record of what a person looked like
choices: Keeping a record of what a person looked like
Showing how wealthy the family who paid for it was
Illustrating scenes from stories everyone already knew
Covering bare walls with patterns
quiz.explain: Portraits were the only way to fix a likeness for children and grandchildren until photography made it quick and cheap.

quiz.prompt: Why do so many of the oldest artworks we still have survive on rock, cave walls or fired clay rather than on cloth or wood?
quiz.answer: Stone and fired clay survive damp, insects and time for thousands of years, while cloth and wood rot away, so what is left to find is mostly the hard material rather than everything that was once made.
quiz.explain: What survives is not what people made most of; it is what lasted, which quietly biases our picture of ancient art.

nodes.title: Color and Composition
nodes.goal: Color wheels, balance and perspective.

quiz.prompt: On a traditional color wheel, if you mix the primary colors blue and yellow, which color do you get?
quiz.answer: Green
quiz.explain: Blue and yellow are primaries that combine to make the secondary color green; orange comes from red and yellow, and purple from red and blue.
choices: Brown
Green
Orange
Purple

quiz.prompt: In linear perspective, railroad tracks running straight away from you appear to come together at a single spot in the distance. What is that spot called?
quiz.answer: The vanishing point
quiz.explain: In linear perspective, parallel lines receding into the distance appear to converge at a vanishing point, which sits on the horizon line but is not the whole line itself.
choices: The far horizon line
The central focus
The foreground plane
The vanishing point

quiz.prompt: A colour wheel is drawn as a circle with the three primary colours and the three secondary colours spaced evenly around it. How many degrees apart is each colour from the next one round the circle?
quiz.explain: Six colours spread evenly round a 360 degree circle sit 360 / 6 = 60 degrees apart, and each secondary sits exactly between the two primaries that make it.

quiz.prompt: A painter wants one red poppy to look as vivid as it possibly can. Which background will make that red burn brightest?
quiz.answer: Green grass, the complement of red
choices: Green grass, the complement of red
Orange autumn leaves
Pale pink blossom
Dark reddish-brown earth
quiz.explain: Red and green sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, and opposite colours sharpen each other. Backgrounds close to red on the wheel, like orange or pink, swallow it instead.

quiz.prompt: You are drawing two friends of the same height on flat ground, one close to you and one far away. In your drawing the horizon crosses the near friend at her shoulders. Where does it cross the far friend?
quiz.answer: At her shoulders too, even though she is drawn much smaller
choices: At her shoulders too, even though she is drawn much smaller
Above her head, because she stands further away
At her feet, because she stands on the horizon
At her knees, since distance pulls the line down
quiz.explain: The horizon sits at your own eye level, so it cuts every person of your height at the same place on the body, near or far. Distance changes their size, not where the line crosses them.

quiz.prompt: A poster has one heavy dark shape in the top-left corner and bare paper everywhere else. The designer says the picture feels as though it is toppling over. What would steady it?
quiz.answer: A smaller shape low on the right, answering it
choices: A smaller shape low on the right, answering it
A second heavy shape in the very same corner
A thin border drawn around the whole poster
A brighter colour for the shape already there
quiz.explain: Balance is about where the visual weight sits. A small shape placed far from the centre can hold up a big one on the other side, the way a light child balances a heavier one further along a see-saw.

quiz.prompt: A painter mixes red and blue, then stirs in white. What colour does she end up with?
quiz.answer: A pale purple
choices: A pale purple
A pale orange
A dark brown
A pale green
quiz.explain: Red and blue make purple, and white lightens whatever it is added to without changing which colour it is.

quiz.prompt: A canvas is 90 cm tall and the horizon is drawn one third of the way up from the bottom. How many centimetres above the bottom edge is the horizon?
quiz.explain: One third of 90 is 30 centimetres.

quiz.prompt: In a landscape the far hills are painted pale bluish grey while the near field is strong green. What does that do for the picture?
quiz.answer: Pushes the hills back, since cool pale colours recede
choices: Pushes the hills back, since cool pale colours recede
Pulls the hills forward, since blue is a powerful colour
Tells the viewer the hills are colder than the field
Flattens the picture, since only two colours are used
quiz.explain: Air between you and a distant object scatters light, so painters copy that fading to create depth on a flat surface.

quiz.prompt: A pupil wants to darken a bright orange, but black makes it look muddy and dead. What should she add instead?
quiz.answer: A little blue, its opposite on the wheel
choices: A little blue, its opposite on the wheel
A little yellow, its neighbour on the wheel
More white, which softens it without muddying
A second thick layer of the same orange
quiz.explain: A colour's complement darkens and calms it while leaving it recognisably orange, where black just drains it.

nodes.title: Reading Music
nodes.goal: Notes, staves, rhythm and time signatures.

quiz.prompt: A piece of music is written in 4/4 time. What does the top number (4) tell you?
quiz.answer: How many beats are in each measure
quiz.explain: In a time signature, the top number gives the number of beats per measure, while the bottom number tells which note value gets one beat.
choices: How fast the music should be played
How many beats are in each measure
How many measures are in the whole song
Which instrument should play

quiz.prompt: In 4/4 time, a quarter note gets one beat. How many quarter notes fit into a single measure?
quiz.explain: 4/4 time has four beats per measure and a quarter note equals one beat, so four quarter notes fill exactly one measure.

quiz.prompt: In 4/4 time a quarter note lasts one beat. A half note is tied to a quarter note, so the two are held as one sound. How many beats does that sound last?
quiz.explain: A half note is worth two beats and a quarter note one, and a tie adds the values together: 2 + 1 = 3 beats held without a new attack.

quiz.prompt: A march is written in 2/4, so each measure holds two quarter-note beats. How many quarter notes fill three complete measures?
quiz.explain: Two quarter notes per measure times three measures gives six. The bottom number names the note that gets the beat; the top number says how many of them fit.

quiz.prompt: A tune is written in 6/8. What does the bottom number tell the player?
quiz.answer: That an eighth note gets one beat
choices: That an eighth note gets one beat
That a measure holds eight beats
That the piece runs for eight measures
That the eighth note is the fastest note allowed
quiz.explain: The bottom number names the note value that counts as one beat, and the top number says how many of them fill a measure. Swapping the two is the most common slip in reading a time signature.

quiz.prompt: A curved line joins a note to the very next note, which sits on the same line of the staff and carries the same letter name. How should the pair be played?
quiz.answer: As a single sound, held for the length of both notes together
choices: As a single sound, held for the length of both notes together
Smoothly joined, but struck a second time
As two separate notes with a gap between them
With a stress on the second of the two notes
quiz.explain: A curve between two notes of the same pitch is a tie: their values are added and the note is sounded once. A curve between different pitches is a slur, which asks for smooth playing, not one long note.

quiz.prompt: In 3/4 time a quarter note lasts one beat. A dot after a note adds half of that note's length again. How many beats does a dotted quarter note last?
quiz.explain: A quarter note is one beat and the dot adds half a beat more, giving 1.5 beats — half a measure of 3/4.

quiz.prompt: In 4/4 time a quarter note lasts one beat and an eighth note lasts half a beat. How many eighth notes fill two complete measures?
quiz.explain: Each measure holds 8 eighth notes, so two measures hold 16.

quiz.prompt: A rest sign is printed on the staff where a note might have been. What does the player do?
quiz.answer: Stay silent for that length of time
choices: Stay silent for that length of time
Play the note more quietly than usual
Hold the previous note for longer
Repeat the whole of the last measure
quiz.explain: A rest is measured silence: the beat carries on being counted, but nothing sounds.

quiz.prompt: Two notes are printed on the same staff, one high up and one low down. What does the height on the staff tell the player?
quiz.answer: How high or low the sound is
choices: How high or low the sound is
How loud the note should be played
How long the note is held
Which finger should play it
quiz.explain: Vertical position on a staff means pitch; loudness comes from separate markings and length comes from the note's shape.

nodes.title: Drama and Theatre
nodes.goal: Act out stories; stagecraft and script.

quiz.prompt: In a play script, the printed lines that tell an actor how to move or where to stand (not the words they speak) are called what?
quiz.answer: Stage directions
quiz.explain: Stage directions are the script's instructions for movement and action, separate from the dialogue that actors speak aloud.
choices: The theatre set
Stage directions
Spoken dialogue
The plot outline

quiz.prompt: In a stage production, who guides the actors' performances and shapes the overall look and interpretation of the show?
quiz.answer: The director
quiz.explain: The director guides the actors and unifies the production's vision, whereas the playwright writes the script and the audience watches.
choices: The usher
The playwright
The director
The audience

quiz.prompt: Two actors are talking to each other in a scene, but the director keeps asking them to turn their bodies part-way towards the seats. Why?
quiz.answer: So the audience can see their faces and hear their voices. An actor who turns fully away sends the sound into the back wall and hides every expression.
quiz.explain: Actors call it cheating out: standing at an angle so the scene still plays to the room. In a film the camera can come to the actor, so this is one of the sharpest differences between screen acting and stage acting.

quiz.prompt: A script says a character exits stage left. You are sitting in the audience looking at the stage. Which way should you expect them to walk off?
quiz.answer: To your right
choices: To your right
Towards the back of the set
Whichever way the actor happens to be facing
To your left
quiz.explain: Stage directions are given from the actor's point of view, facing the audience, so stage left is the audience's right. Upstage and downstage name the back and the front of the stage for the same reason.

quiz.prompt: In the second act an actor picks up a letter, reads it aloud and tears it in half. A fresh letter has to be waiting before every performance. Whose job is that?
quiz.answer: The props manager, who supplies and resets the objects actors handle
choices: The props manager, who supplies and resets the objects actors handle
The set designer, who builds the walls and furniture
The costume maker, who dresses each character
The lighting operator, who lights the scene
quiz.explain: Anything an actor picks up and uses is a prop, and props that get eaten, torn or broken have to be replaced for each show. The set is what the actors move around in; props are what they move.

quiz.prompt: A playwright and a film director tell the same story of a family argument. The play keeps everything in one kitchen; the film can cut to the street, the hospital and a memory from ten years ago. What must the playwright lean on more heavily?
quiz.answer: What the characters say aloud, since nothing else is shown
choices: What the characters say aloud, since nothing else is shown
Cuts between places, to keep the pace up
Close-ups of faces, so feelings can be read
Music under the scene, to carry the mood
quiz.explain: Since the audience is shown only the kitchen. A stage holds one place at a time, so a playwright has to put the street, the hospital and the past into speech. Film can simply show them, which is why plays usually carry far more talk per minute than films do.

quiz.prompt: A company rehearses a play for six weeks before any audience sees it. What is the main reason?
quiz.answer: So the company can deliver the same show every night
choices: So the company can deliver the same show every night
A theatre has to be booked that far in advance
The actors need that long to learn all their lines
The costumes take about six weeks to sew
quiz.explain: A performance has to be repeatable, so rehearsal turns choices into something the company can deliver reliably. Lines are usually learned in the first week; what takes six is everything built on top of them.

quiz.prompt: A play has 3 acts. Each act contains 4 scenes, and every scene begins with one lighting change. How many lighting changes are cued in the whole play?
quiz.explain: 3 acts times 4 scenes gives 12 scenes, so 12 cues.

quiz.prompt: In a comedy an actor waits two seconds before the last word of a joke, and the laugh gets bigger. Which stage skill is being used?
quiz.answer: Timing
choices: Timing
Projection
Blocking
Diction
quiz.explain: Timing is the control of pace and pause; the pause lets the audience get ahead of the joke, which sharpens the punchline.

quiz.prompt: A small theatre seats its audience on all four sides of the acting area. What must the director do differently from an ordinary end-on stage?
quiz.answer: Keep the actors moving and turning so every side sees a face
choices: Keep the actors moving and turning so every side sees a face
Have the actors speak much louder, since the room is larger
Arrange every scene so all four sides see each face at once
Place all the scenery against the back wall
quiz.explain: So no one side gets the whole show. In the round there is no single front, so a fixed facing would leave three quarters of the audience watching a back. Showing every face to every side at once is impossible, which is why the staging keeps moving.

nodes.title: Photography & Film
nodes.goal: Framing an image; how movies are made.

quiz.prompt: A framing guideline suggests placing your main subject off-center, along lines that divide the frame into thirds, instead of dead center. What is this guideline called?
quiz.answer: The rule of thirds
quiz.explain: The rule of thirds improves composition by aligning subjects with lines that split the frame into thirds; the others describe lighting, focus, and camera motion.
choices: The rule of thirds
The golden hour
The depth of field
The panning shot

quiz.prompt: A movie is really a long series of still pictures shown very quickly, one after another. Why do we see smooth motion instead of separate pictures?
quiz.answer: The images change faster than our eyes can follow
quiz.explain: Film shows still frames rapidly (about 24 per second), and because they change faster than the eye resolves them, they fuse into the illusion of continuous motion. The strip moves in jerks, one frame at a time, with the shutter closed in between.
choices: The projector blurs each picture into the next as it moves
Each frame records the motion that happened while it was exposed
The film is one long picture pulled steadily past the lens
The images change faster than our eyes can follow

quiz.prompt: A film is shown at 24 still pictures, called frames, every second. How many separate frames make up a shot that lasts 10 seconds?
quiz.explain: 24 frames a second for 10 seconds is 240 frames. A two-hour film runs to well over 170,000 of them, each one a photograph.

quiz.prompt: You photograph a friend standing in front of a big sunny window. In the picture her face comes out almost black, while the window looks fine. What happened?
quiz.answer: The camera set itself for the bright window
choices: The camera set itself for the bright window
The camera focused on the window instead of on her
The lens was smudged with a fingerprint
She moved a little as the picture was taken
quiz.explain: So her darker face went dark. A camera picks one brightness for the whole frame. Set for the window, everything dimmer than the window records as shadow, which is why photographers turn the subject towards the light or add some of their own.

quiz.prompt: In a photo of a running dog, the dog is a smear while the fence behind it stays sharp. Which change would fix the smear?
quiz.answer: A faster shutter speed, to freeze the motion
choices: A faster shutter speed, to freeze the motion
A careful refocus on the dog's eye
A step or two further back from the dog
A slower shutter speed to gather more light
quiz.explain: Only the moving thing is smeared, so the problem is time, not focus: the shutter stayed open while the dog travelled. A shorter exposure freezes it; a longer one smears it further.

quiz.prompt: A film crew shoots the last scene of the film on Monday and the first scene on Friday. The actors are not confused and the film still makes sense. Why work that way?
quiz.answer: Every scene set in one place is shot together, then cut back into story order
choices: Every scene set in one place is shot together, then cut back into story order
The ending matters most, so it is filmed while everyone is fresh
Actors remember their last lines best
The story is written after the filming is finished
quiz.explain: Sets, locations and lighting are the expensive things, so a schedule groups shots by place rather than by plot. Editing puts the story back in order afterwards.

quiz.prompt: The same tree is photographed at noon under flat overhead sun and again at sunset in long low light. Which photo shows its shape and texture more strongly?
quiz.answer: The sunset photo, whose low sun casts long shadows
choices: The sunset photo, whose low sun casts long shadows
The noon photo, because more light reaches the tree
The noon photo, because sunset shadows hide the detail
Neither, since it is the same tree in both pictures
quiz.explain: Shadow is what tells a flat picture about depth, so raking light describes a surface that flat light flattens.

quiz.prompt: A film runs at 24 frames every second. A shot uses 180 frames. How many seconds long is it?
quiz.explain: 180 divided by 24 gives 7.5 seconds.

quiz.prompt: Instead of standing over a small child, a photographer crouches and shoots from her eye level. What changes in the picture?
quiz.answer: She is shown as an equal rather than being looked down on
choices: She is shown as an equal rather than being looked down on
The picture comes out sharper, since crouching holds the camera steadier
The background disappears out of the frame
She looks taller than she really is, since you are below her
quiz.explain: Camera height is a point of view in both senses: looking down makes a subject small, and eye level meets them.

quiz.prompt: In a portrait, a lamp in the background appears to grow out of the top of the subject's head. Which change fixes it?
quiz.answer: Step sideways so the lamp no longer lines up behind her
choices: Step sideways so the lamp no longer lines up behind her
Use a faster shutter speed to sharpen the lamp
Zoom in so that the lamp appears larger
Brighten the whole picture so that the lamp blends into the wall behind
quiz.explain: A photograph flattens depth, so anything behind the subject can seem attached; moving the camera separates them.

nodes.title: Art History
nodes.goal: Movements from the Renaissance to today.

quiz.prompt: Which of these art movements appeared earliest in history?
quiz.answer: Impressionism
quiz.explain: Impressionism arose in the 1870s, before Cubism (about 1907), Surrealism (1920s), and Pop art (1950s-60s).
choices: Surrealist art
Early Cubism
Pop art prints
Impressionism

quiz.prompt: A painting shows a single guitar broken into flat, angular planes, as if you were seeing it from several viewpoints at once. Which movement does this best fit?
quiz.answer: Cubism
quiz.explain: Cubism fragmented objects into geometric planes and combined multiple viewpoints in one image, unlike the realistic depth of Renaissance or Baroque work.
choices: Baroque
Renaissance
Impressionism
Cubism

quiz.prompt: A Renaissance painting of a religious scene is admired for its balanced arrangement and convincing sense of depth. Which technique, revived in the Renaissance, created that realistic depth?
quiz.answer: Linear perspective
quiz.explain: Renaissance artists systematized linear perspective to create believable spatial depth on a flat surface, a hallmark of the era.
choices: Impressionist brushwork
Linear perspective
Abstract color fields
Cubist fragmentation

quiz.prompt: The first Impressionist group exhibition opened in Paris in 1874. Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, the canvas that opens Cubism, in 1907. How many years separate the two?
quiz.explain: 1907 - 1874 = 33 years. Two generations covered the distance from broken sunlight to broken form.

quiz.prompt: Monet painted the same haystack more than twenty times, changing nothing but the hour and the season. What was he recording?
quiz.answer: The light on the stack, which recolours everything it falls on
choices: The light on the stack, which recolours everything it falls on
The slow decay of the stack across a whole year
Practice attempts, until the drawing finally came right
The farm's year, from harvest through to winter feeding
quiz.explain: The series exists because the subject is not the hay. Holding the object fixed lets the changing light become the visible content, which is the Impressionist wager in its purest form.

quiz.prompt: In 1950 Jackson Pollock laid a huge canvas on the floor and poured and flicked house paint across it, walking round all four sides. No object appears anywhere in the finished picture. What is a viewer being asked to attend to?
quiz.answer: The painter's movement, recorded in the loops and pools of paint
choices: The painter's movement, recorded in the loops and pools of paint
A hidden picture that appears once you stand far enough back
Chance patterns, made by paint left to fall where it liked
A design worked out on paper first and then poured carefully
quiz.explain: With no image to read, what remains is the trace of the act: speed, reach, the moment paint left the stick. Critics called it action painting for that reason. Pollock worked without a drawn plan, but he was not simply letting the paint fall where it liked either.

quiz.prompt: An Impressionist worked outdoors in an hour with broken visible brushstrokes, while an academic painter spent months in a studio building a smooth invisible finish. What did the Impressionist gain?
quiz.answer: A record of one changing moment of light
choices: A record of one changing moment of light
A more exact drawing of the subject's outline
A cheaper picture, since less paint was used
A bigger canvas than a studio could hold
quiz.explain: Painting fast and outdoors was a method chosen to catch conditions that would be gone by the afternoon.

quiz.prompt: The High Renaissance in Italy is usually dated from about 1495 to about 1520. How many years does that span cover?
quiz.explain: 1520 minus 1495 is 25 years.

quiz.prompt: A Baroque painting throws one figure into a shaft of light while the rest of the room falls into deep shadow. What is that device called, and what does it do?
quiz.answer: Chiaroscuro, which models form and steers the eye
choices: Chiaroscuro, which models form and steers the eye
Sfumato, which softens every edge into haze
Impasto, which builds the paint into thick ridges
Fresco, which fixes the colour into wet plaster
quiz.explain: Chiaroscuro is the strong opposition of light and dark; the other three terms name a blending, a paint texture and a technique of wall painting.

quiz.prompt: Duchamp exhibited a shop-bought bottle rack as sculpture. Which claim about art does that gesture press hardest?
quiz.answer: That choosing and placing can matter more than making by hand
choices: That choosing and placing can matter more than making by hand
That a machine-made object can be finished better than a hand-carved one
That sculpture ought to be useful as well as beautiful to look at
That anything placed in a gallery becomes art by that fact alone
quiz.explain: The readymade shifts the artist's work from craft to selection, and puts the question to the gallery rather than the object.

nodes.title: Music Theory
nodes.goal: Scales, keys, chords and harmony.

quiz.prompt: A major triad uses the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of its major scale. The C major triad is C-E-G. Using the same pattern on the G major scale (G-A-B-C-D-E-F#), which notes make the G major triad?
quiz.answer: G-B-D
quiz.explain: The 1st, 3rd, and 5th degrees of the G major scale are G, B, and D, giving the G major triad G-B-D.
choices: G-A-D
G-B-F
G-B-D
G-C-E

quiz.prompt: Every major key shares its exact set of notes with a relative minor key. C major has no sharps or flats. Which minor key shares those same notes?
quiz.answer: A minor
quiz.explain: A minor is the relative minor of C major; both use only the white keys, with A minor's keynote lying three half-steps below C.
choices: E minor
G minor
A minor
D minor

quiz.prompt: You play the note C and then the G directly above it, spanning the letters C-D-E-F-G. What is this interval called?
quiz.answer: A fifth
quiz.explain: Counting inclusively from C to G gives five letter names, making the interval a (perfect) fifth.
choices: A fourth
An octave
A fifth
A third

quiz.prompt: A string 60 cm long sounds the note C. Pressed so that only two thirds of its length can vibrate, it sounds the G a perfect fifth above. How many centimetres are vibrating?
quiz.explain: Two thirds of 60 cm is 40 cm. A perfect fifth is the length ratio 3:2, which is why it sounds so settled: the two waves line up every few cycles.

quiz.prompt: A song sits in C major but runs too low for the singer, so every note is moved up by three semitones. Which key does the song end up in?
quiz.answer: E flat major
choices: E flat major
D major
E major
F major
quiz.explain: Three semitones above C is E flat (C to C sharp to D to E flat). D is two semitones up and E is four, so both come from counting the steps rather than the semitones.

quiz.prompt: A major triad stacks four semitones and then three, as C-E-G does. A minor triad swaps that order: three semitones, then four. Which notes make the A minor triad?
quiz.answer: A, C, E
choices: A, C, E
A, B, E
A, C, E flat
A, C sharp, E
quiz.explain: Three semitones above A is C, and four above C is E. Raising the middle note to C sharp would give A major; lowering the top note to E flat would give a diminished triad.

quiz.prompt: How many semitones lie between C and the F directly above it?
quiz.explain: C to C sharp, D, D sharp, E and F is five semitone steps, which is a perfect fourth.

quiz.prompt: A piece in G major carries one sharp in its key signature. Which note is sharpened?
quiz.answer: F sharp
choices: C sharp
F sharp
G sharp
B flat
quiz.explain: The G major scale needs a semitone between its seventh and eighth notes, which requires F sharp rather than F natural.

quiz.prompt: The dominant seventh chord in C major is G-B-D-F. Why does it pull so strongly back to a C chord?
quiz.answer: The tritone B-F resolves inward to C and E
choices: The tritone B-F resolves inward to C and E
It carries a note from outside the key, which has to be corrected
It has four notes rather than three, and four notes cannot settle
It shares no notes at all with the C chord
quiz.explain: The tension comes from the tritone B-F, whose two notes each move by a semitone into the tonic chord. Every note of G-B-D-F belongs to C major, and the chord shares its G with the C triad, so neither a foreign note nor the count of notes explains the pull.

quiz.prompt: A choir sings a melody, then sings it again starting a fourth higher, keeping every interval the same. What has been done to the melody?
quiz.answer: It has been transposed
choices: It has been transposed
It has been inverted
It has been syncopated
It has been augmented
quiz.explain: Transposition shifts every pitch by the same interval; inversion flips the direction of each step and augmentation stretches the rhythm.

nodes.title: Design & Architecture
nodes.goal: Form and function in objects and buildings.

quiz.prompt: The design principle 'form follows function' means that:
quiz.answer: An object's shape should follow the job it must do
quiz.explain: 'Form follows function' holds that the purpose of an object should shape its design. It is a claim about what drives the form, not a ban on ornament and not a ranking of beauty against use.
choices: An object's job should be settled after its shape is chosen
An object's shape should follow the job it must do
A beautiful shape always matters more than usefulness
A well-designed object should carry no decoration at all

quiz.prompt: You are designing a teapot. Which choice best reflects good functional design?
quiz.answer: A cool handle and a spout that pours without dripping
quiz.explain: Each of the other three is a real design choice that looks well and then fails in the hand: a teapot has to pour cleanly, hold its lid and be safe to grip, so the form has to serve the use.
choices: A wide flat lid that looks handsome but slips when the pot tilts
A slim spout that suits the silhouette but pours very slowly
A cool handle and a spout that pours without dripping
A metal handle that matches the body and heats with the tea

quiz.prompt: On a poster, the title is set large and bold while the details are small, so the eye knows what to read first. This deliberate ordering of importance is called visual:
quiz.answer: Hierarchy
quiz.explain: Visual hierarchy uses size, weight, and placement to guide the viewer's attention through information in order of importance.
choices: Proportion
Hierarchy
Symmetry
Saturation

quiz.prompt: A designer wants a poster whose short side is 34 cm and whose sides stand in the golden ratio, taken as 1.618. How long is the long side, to the nearest centimetre?
quiz.explain: 34 x 1.618 = 55.0 cm. 34 and 55 are neighbours in the Fibonacci sequence, and dividing one Fibonacci number by the one before it closes in on the golden ratio.

quiz.prompt: A glass door carries a flat metal plate on one face and a long vertical bar on the other. People walk up and push the plate side without reading anything. What is the plate doing?
quiz.answer: Telling the hand what to do: with nothing to grip, the only move it offers is a push
choices: Telling the hand what to do: with nothing to grip, the only move it offers is a push
Marking which half of the door carries the hinges
Protecting the glass from greasy fingerprints
Holding the two sheets of glass together
quiz.explain: A shape that announces its own use is called an affordance: a plate affords pushing, a bar affords pulling. A door that needs a PUSH sticker is a door whose form is fighting its function.

quiz.prompt: A design is to be printed as a linocut: ink is rolled across the surface of the block, and whatever the knife cuts away prints as bare paper. Which drawing survives that process best?
quiz.answer: Bold flat shapes with thick lines
choices: Bold flat shapes with thick lines
A faded photograph in pale grey
A soft pencil sketch full of grey shading
Hairline cross-hatching over the whole design
quiz.explain: Relief printing gives ink or nothing, with no half-tones, and every white mark has to be cut out by hand. Knowing what the process cannot do shapes the drawing before the knife touches the block.

quiz.prompt: A kettle's handle is fitted directly above the spout, and users scald their hands in the escaping steam. What has gone wrong?
quiz.answer: The shape ignores how the object is actually used
choices: The shape ignores how the object is actually used
The parts are not arranged in a clear visual hierarchy
The handle is too small for an adult hand to grip
The kettle looks unbalanced when seen from the side
quiz.explain: Form following function means the use comes first: a handle has to be somewhere a hand can safely be. Grip size and balance are real faults too, but neither of them is what is scalding anyone here.

quiz.prompt: A page is 210 mm wide with 20 mm margins on each side and two equal columns separated by a 10 mm gutter. How many millimetres wide is each column?
quiz.explain: 210 minus the two 20 mm margins and the 10 mm gutter leaves 160 mm, split into two columns of 80 mm.

quiz.prompt: A glass office wall faces the afternoon sun and the rooms behind it overheat. Which response treats the cause rather than the symptom?
quiz.answer: Deep shading fitted outside the glass
choices: Deep shading fitted outside the glass
A larger air-conditioning plant
Thicker carpet and internal blinds
Opening the windows on the shaded side of the building
quiz.explain: Once sunlight is inside the glass its heat is already in the room, so the shade has to intercept it outside.

quiz.prompt: Why do designers test a rough paper prototype with real users before anything is built?
quiz.answer: Because a problem found early is cheap to change while everything is still on paper, and watching real users reveals confusions the designer cannot predict from the drawing, since the designer already knows how it is meant to work.
quiz.explain: Prototyping buys information at the point where changing your mind still costs nothing.

nodes.title: History of Music
nodes.goal: Baroque, Classical, Romantic, jazz and beyond.

quiz.prompt: Which of these musical eras came earliest in time?
quiz.answer: Baroque
quiz.explain: The order is Baroque (roughly 1600-1750), then Classical, then Romantic, with jazz emerging in the early 20th century.
choices: Classical
Jazz
Baroque
Romantic

quiz.prompt: Johann Sebastian Bach, famous for his intricate fugues and harpsichord works, is a central composer of which era?
quiz.answer: The Baroque era
quiz.explain: Bach (1685-1750) is a defining figure of the Baroque era, known for complex counterpoint like the fugue.
choices: The Classical era
The Romantic era
The Jazz era
The Baroque era

quiz.prompt: A small group plays a familiar tune, and then each musician takes turns inventing brand-new melodies over the chords on the spot. This emphasis on improvisation is a hallmark of:
quiz.answer: Jazz
quiz.explain: Spontaneous improvisation over a tune's chord changes is a defining feature of jazz.
choices: Gregorian chant
Classical symphony
Jazz
Baroque

quiz.prompt: A minuet runs for 48 bars of 3/4, and the conductor beats 144 quarter-note beats a minute. How many seconds does it last?
quiz.explain: 48 bars x 3 beats = 144 beats, and at 144 beats a minute that is exactly one minute. Tempo marks turn a page of bars into a length of time.

quiz.prompt: In a Baroque concerto grosso the music swings back and forth between a handful of soloists and the whole band, and the loudness changes in sudden steps rather than by swelling. What does that arrangement give a listener?
quiz.answer: A conversation between a small group and a large one, with every join audible
choices: A conversation between a small group and a large one, with every join audible
A slow build from quiet to loud across the movement
One melody played by the whole band at once
A steady speeding up towards the final bar
quiz.explain: Terraced dynamics come from the forces themselves: fewer players, softer; everyone in, louder. The gradual swell that Romantic music lives on was not yet the main tool of the trade.

quiz.prompt: In a Haydn quartet the first violin carries the tune while the other three supply chords beneath it. In a Bach fugue all four voices take up the same subject in turn and each goes its own way. How do the two textures differ?
quiz.answer: Tune plus backing, against four independent lines
choices: Tune plus backing, against four independent lines
One sits in a major key and the other in a minor key
One uses strings and the other needs a keyboard
One stays loud throughout and the other stays quiet
quiz.explain: Haydn's texture is homophonic: one melody, everything else supporting. Bach's is polyphonic: several melodies of equal standing at the same time. The difference is in how many things are worth following, not in key or instrument.

quiz.prompt: What most clearly separates a Romantic symphony from a Classical one?
quiz.answer: A bigger orchestra and wider extremes
choices: A bigger orchestra and wider extremes
A harpsichord playing continuously to keep the time
Shorter movements played by fewer instruments
Improvised solos over a repeating chord pattern
quiz.explain: The Romantic century expanded the orchestra and the emotional range; continuo harpsichord belongs to the Baroque before it.

quiz.prompt: Bach was born in 1685 and Beethoven in 1770. How many years separate the two births?
quiz.explain: 1770 minus 1685 is 85 years.

quiz.prompt: A jazz group plays head, then solos, then head again. What happens in the middle section?
quiz.answer: Players improvise new melodies over the tune's chord changes
choices: Players improvise new melodies over the tune's chord changes
Each player performs the same written melody in turn from the top
The whole band plays a passage written out beforehand
The drummer keeps a pattern going while no harmony sounds underneath
quiz.explain: The head states the tune; the solos keep its harmony as a shared framework while the melody is invented afresh.

quiz.prompt: Recording was invented in the late nineteenth century. Which of its effects on music reached furthest?
quiz.answer: A performance could be heard far from the room it happened in
choices: A performance could be heard far from the room it happened in
Songs were shaped to fit the three minutes a disc would hold
Orchestras grew larger so that they could be heard clearly at the back
Music became slower to suit the machines of the day
quiz.explain: Recording cut the link between hearing music and being present, which changed who could hear what, and where.

nodes.title: Film & Media
nodes.goal: How film tells stories; genres and technique.

quiz.prompt: A film cuts from a character's frightened face to a growling dog, then back to the face. By placing these shots side by side, the editing makes us feel the character fears the dog. This power of shot arrangement to create meaning is called:
quiz.answer: Montage
quiz.explain: Montage (the Kuleshov effect) shows that meaning emerges from how shots are edited together, not just from each shot alone.
choices: Casting
Framing
Montage
Lighting

quiz.prompt: A film features a lone gunslinger, dusty frontier towns, and horseback showdowns at high noon. These conventions place it in which genre?
quiz.answer: Western
quiz.explain: Gunslingers, frontier settings, and showdowns are classic conventions of the Western genre.
choices: Musical
Western
Film noir
Documentary

quiz.prompt: At an emotional moment, a director wants the audience to clearly notice a single tear on a character's cheek. Which shot best achieves this?
quiz.answer: A close-up
quiz.explain: A close-up fills the frame with a small detail like a face, drawing the viewer's attention to subtle emotion.
choices: A wide shot
A close-up
A long shot
An aerial shot

quiz.prompt: A 90-minute film is cut from 1,200 shots. What is the average shot length, in seconds?
quiz.explain: 90 minutes is 5,400 seconds, and 5,400 / 1,200 = 4.5 seconds a shot. Average shot length is a real measure of style: 1940s films often run 10 seconds or more, modern action films under 3.

quiz.prompt: Two characters face each other across a table. The crew films one over each shoulder from the same side of the room, then carries the camera to the far side of the table for the next line. What do the two shots do when cut together?
quiz.answer: The two seem to swap sides of the screen and stop looking at each other
choices: The two seem to swap sides of the screen and stop looking at each other
Nothing changes, because the faces look the same in both shots
The scene seems to jump forward in time
One character seems to have moved into the other's chair
quiz.explain: Crossing the imaginary line between two characters reverses screen direction, so eyelines no longer meet. Keeping the camera on one side of that line is the 180-degree rule, and breaking it deliberately is how directors unsettle a scene.

quiz.prompt: Early in a film a woman switches on her car radio and a song plays. An hour later the same song plays over a shot of her walking alone, with no radio anywhere. What has changed about the song?
quiz.answer: It has moved outside the story world, heard only by us
choices: It has moved outside the story world, heard only by us
It has become a voice-over spoken by the character
It is now played by an orchestra somewhere in the scene
It has turned diegetic, part of the world she can hear inside the car
quiz.explain: Sound the characters can hear is diegetic; sound only the audience hears is not. Moving a song across that line is a standard trick, because the audience remembers where the tune came from.

quiz.prompt: A scene cuts from a wide shot of a street, to a close-up of a hand on a door handle, to the character's eyes. What is the audience being given?
quiz.answer: An order of attention
choices: An order of attention
A signal that hours have passed since the last scene
A signal that the scene is a memory
A hint that someone else is watching the character
quiz.explain: Editing controls attention. A wide shot places you, a detail tells you what counts, and a reaction tells you how to feel about it.

quiz.prompt: A film is shot at 24 frames every second. A chase lasts 3 minutes. How many frames are exposed?
quiz.explain: 3 minutes is 180 seconds, and 180 times 24 gives 4,320 frames.

quiz.prompt: A director films an entire conversation in one unbroken take with a moving camera. What does that gain over cutting between shots?
quiz.answer: Unbroken real time and space, so the tension never resets
choices: Unbroken real time and space, so the tension never resets
A quicker edit, since there is nothing left to cut together
Freedom to repair a weak moment later in the cutting room
Tighter control over exactly which detail the audience notices
quiz.explain: A long take keeps the scene continuous, but it gives up the pinpoint control of attention that cutting provides, and the safety net with it: with no cuts there is nothing to cut around.

quiz.prompt: A camera set low looks up at a character who fills the frame. What does that angle most commonly convey?
quiz.answer: Power
choices: Power
Weakness
Confusion
Distance
quiz.explain: Looking up at someone puts the viewer in the position of a smaller person, which reads as dominance.

nodes.title: Aesthetics
nodes.goal: The philosophy of beauty and taste.

quiz.prompt: The saying 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder' expresses which view about beauty?
quiz.answer: Beauty depends on the individual's own response
quiz.explain: The phrase captures aesthetic subjectivism, the view that judgments of beauty depend on the perceiver rather than on a fixed property of the object.
choices: Beauty depends on the individual's own response
Beauty can always be measured by science alone
Beauty is a fixed property of the object itself
Only trained experts are able to perceive beauty

quiz.prompt: Kant argued that a genuine judgment of beauty is 'disinterested.' In his sense, a disinterested pleasure is one that:
quiz.answer: Does not rest on the object's use or on our desires
quiz.explain: For Kant, disinterested pleasure is delight in an object's form apart from any personal use or desire, which is what makes it a pure aesthetic judgment.
choices: Is felt only by people who are bored or uninterested
Does not rest on the object's use or on our desires
Arises mainly from owning or possessing the object
Is a dull pleasure, felt with no real emotion at all

quiz.prompt: Two friends disagree about whether a song is beautiful, and neither can prove the other wrong. An aesthetic subjectivist would most likely say:
quiz.answer: There may be no objective fact settling who is right
quiz.explain: Subjectivism holds that beauty depends on individual response, so such disagreements need not have one objectively correct answer.
choices: One of them must be simply mistaken about the facts
There may be no objective fact settling who is right
The louder song is by definition the more beautiful one
Beauty can be measured precisely to decide the winner

quiz.prompt: People pay to watch plays that leave them shaken and in tears, yet they take some trouble to avoid grief in ordinary life. Philosophers call this the paradox of tragedy. Set out what any solution to it has to explain.
quiz.answer: Why audiences deliberately seek out works that produce painful emotions such as pity and fear, and find the experience worth having, when they avoid those same feelings outside the theatre.
quiz.explain: The puzzle is not that art moves us but that we choose to be moved this way. Answers on offer include control (the grief is not ours), the pleasure of form, and the value of rehearsing feelings we will one day meet for real.

quiz.prompt: Hume grants that beauty lies in the sentiment of the observer, yet he denies that every verdict carries equal weight. The standard he appeals to comes from:
quiz.answer: the settled verdict of critics with practice, comparison and freedom from prejudice
choices: the settled verdict of critics with practice, comparison and freedom from prejudice
a majority vote taken among ordinary audiences
the proportions a geometer can measure in the object
the price the work commands from serious collectors
quiz.explain: Hume's true judges are made, not born: delicacy of perception, wide comparison, practice and a mind free of prejudice. That lets him keep beauty in the response while still ranking Milton above a hack.

quiz.prompt: A porcelain urinal stands in a plumbing showroom; a near-identical one, signed R. Mutt, stands on a plinth in a gallery. An institutional theorist explains the difference by pointing to:
quiz.answer: the artworld that confers the status
choices: the artworld that confers the status
the greater skill used to make the gallery piece
the signature, which turns any object into a work
the beauty a trained eye can find in the gallery piece
quiz.explain: On Dickie's account, being art is a status conferred by a practice and its institutions, not a quality you could detect by inspecting the porcelain. That is why the showroom twin stays plumbing.

quiz.prompt: A collector learns that the landscape she has loved for years is a forgery painted last decade, though nothing about the surface has altered. Her pleasure collapses. Which position does that reaction support?
quiz.answer: That a work's value depends partly on its origin, not on appearance alone
choices: That a work's value depends partly on its origin, not on appearance alone
That beauty is wholly a matter of the viewer's passing mood on a given day
That a forgery is invariably weaker in execution than the original it copies
That only trained experts can experience beauty at all
quiz.explain: If appearance were everything, learning the date could not change the verdict; the reaction suggests provenance is part of the object of appreciation.

quiz.prompt: A viewer calls a violent film superbly made yet morally repellent, and refuses to count it as good art. Which philosophical dispute does the case stage?
quiz.answer: Whether moral flaws are aesthetic flaws
choices: Whether moral flaws are aesthetic flaws
Whether film is capable of being art at all
Whether galleries ought to censor what audiences may see
Whether technical skill can be measured objectively
quiz.explain: This is the moralism debate: autonomists keep the two verdicts separate, while moderate moralists hold that a moral flaw can spoil the work as art.

quiz.prompt: Two critics agree on every describable feature of a poem and still disagree about whether it is beautiful. Explain why that makes beauty awkward to treat as an ordinary property of the object.
quiz.answer: If all the descriptive features are settled and the verdict still divides, beauty cannot simply be read off those features the way a shape or a colour can; the judgement depends on a response the critic brings to the poem, which is why taste resists proof by description alone.
quiz.explain: This gap between description and evaluation is why aesthetic judgements are often called non-inferential: reasons persuade, but they do not compel.

quiz.prompt: A designer argues that a well-made spoon can succeed aesthetically as fully as a sculpture. Which claim does she have to defend?
quiz.answer: That serving a use does not disqualify an object from aesthetic judgement
choices: That serving a use does not disqualify an object from aesthetic judgement
That sculpture serves no purpose whatsoever
That beauty and usefulness amount to the same thing
That craft skill counts for more than the maker's intention when a work is judged
quiz.explain: The obstacle is the Kantian association of aesthetic judgement with disinterest, which functional objects seem to violate.

nodes.title: Art Criticism & Theory
nodes.goal: Reading art critically across cultures.

quiz.prompt: In a fifteenth-century Annunciation, a white lily stands in a vase, a walled garden shows through the window, and Mary wears blue. A scholar argues that none of this is decoration. Reading a picture that way belongs to:
quiz.answer: iconography
choices: iconography
formal analysis, which weighs shape, colour and arrangement
connoisseurship, which assigns the panel to a hand
conservation, which reads the layers beneath the surface
quiz.explain: Which recovers what such motifs meant to a picture's first audience. The lily carries purity, the walled garden virginity, the blue the Virgin herself. Iconography reconstructs that vocabulary; formal analysis would describe the same lily as a white vertical accent and stop there.

quiz.prompt: A critic examines only a painting's lines, colors, shapes, and arrangement, deliberately setting aside its history and subject matter. This approach is called:
quiz.answer: Formal analysis
quiz.explain: Formal analysis focuses on the visual elements and composition themselves, apart from historical or biographical context.
choices: Formal analysis
Social history of art
Iconography
Biographical criticism

quiz.prompt: A scholar working in 'visual culture' would most likely study:
quiz.answer: Everyday images like ads and memes, plus fine art
quiz.explain: Visual culture broadens the study of images beyond fine art to include the full range of everyday visual media.
choices: Everyday images like ads and memes, plus fine art
Only the masterpieces hanging in major art museums
The private life stories of a few famous painters
The prices that artworks fetch at big auction houses

quiz.prompt: An art historian asks what a painting's first audience would have recognised, rather than trusting how the picture strikes a viewer today. Give the reason that method exists.
quiz.answer: Because the meanings carried by symbols and conventions shift over time: the first audience shared a context of codes that we have lost, so reconstructing it recovers meanings a modern eye reads straight past.
quiz.explain: A skull, a lily, a dog at the foot of a bed: each was legible to its own century and is nearly mute now. The method does not forbid a modern response; it stops us mistaking our response for the picture's content.

quiz.prompt: Berger argues that the European oil painting of the female nude composes its subject for a spectator-owner standing outside the frame. Which observation about those paintings would most strengthen his claim?
quiz.answer: The woman gazes out of the canvas, not at anyone in the scene
choices: The woman gazes out of the canvas, not at anyone in the scene
The canvases were often very large and hung high on a wall
Oil paint dries slowly, so a picture took months to finish
Many of the models were paid professionals who posed repeatedly
quiz.explain: Evidence has to bear on the specific claim, which is about how the picture is composed. Size, medium and studio economics are all true of these paintings and none of them shows an address to someone outside the frame.

quiz.prompt: A poet says her poem mourns her father. A critic argues that the text supports a reading about migration instead. Wimsatt and Beardsley's charge of the intentional fallacy would have us conclude that:
quiz.answer: the poet's stated aim does not settle what the poem means
choices: the poet's stated aim does not settle what the poem means
the poet has the last word, since she wrote it
the critic must show that the poet was lying
the poem means whatever any reader takes from it
quiz.explain: The argument is that a poem is public once written, so evidence about meaning comes from the words. It does not license the opposite extreme either: the fourth reading abandons the text just as thoroughly as the first.

quiz.prompt: A museum shows a Benin bronze taken during a punitive expedition, captioned only with its style and date. Which critical approach challenges that caption most directly?
quiz.answer: Postcolonial critique, which asks how the object arrived and who now speaks for it
choices: Postcolonial critique, which asks how the object arrived and who now speaks for it
Formal analysis, which attends only to the modelling of line, mass and surface in the object
Iconography, which decodes the figures and their attributes
Connoisseurship, which attributes the casting to a workshop
quiz.explain: The other three take the object as given; only the postcolonial reading makes the route into the vitrine part of what is on display.

quiz.prompt: A curator enlarges a 1930s documentary photograph of a sharecropper family into a fine-art print for a gallery wall. A critic objects that the setting changes the work. What is the strongest version of that objection?
quiz.answer: The gallery turns a document into taste
choices: The gallery turns a document into taste
The photograph loses definition when it is enlarged that far
Photographs cannot properly be exhibited as artworks
The photographer's original intention can never be known
quiz.explain: The complaint is about the institution, not the print: how a viewer is invited to look is part of what the image now means.

quiz.prompt: A historian notes how few women appear in a canonical survey text. A colleague replies that quality alone decided who was included. Which line of argument answers that reply best?
quiz.answer: That training, patronage and exhibition shaped who could compete
choices: That training, patronage and exhibition shaped who could compete
That work by women has always been of higher quality
That questions of quality cannot meaningfully be discussed at all
That surveys should leave out men until the count has been levelled
quiz.explain: Linda Nochlin's argument moves the question from talent to institutions: the canon records who was allowed to compete.

quiz.prompt: A battle painting is praised by one critic for its accuracy and read by another as propaganda. Explain how both readings can rest on the very same picture.
quiz.answer: Accuracy concerns whether the depicted details match the event, while propaganda concerns what the composition, scale and viewpoint persuade a viewer to feel, so a picture can be factually correct in every detail and still be arranged so that one side appears heroic.
quiz.explain: Selection and arrangement carry an argument even when nothing depicted is false, which is why documentary status settles less than it seems to.

nodes.title: Composition & Analysis
nodes.goal: Counterpoint, form and analyzing scores.

quiz.prompt: In music, counterpoint is the art of:
quiz.answer: Weaving independent melodies that fit together
quiz.explain: Counterpoint interweaves independent melodies that are harmonically interdependent yet rhythmically and melodically distinct.
choices: Weaving independent melodies that fit together
Playing a single melody as loudly as possible
Repeating a single note steadily beneath a tune
Stacking several notes into a single block chord

quiz.prompt: Classical sonata form is traditionally built from three main sections. What is their order?
quiz.answer: Exposition, development, recapitulation
quiz.explain: Sonata form presents themes in the exposition, transforms them in the development, and restates them in the recapitulation.
choices: Exposition, development, recapitulation
Introduction, solo section, final coda
Opening verse, chorus, and closing bridge
Main theme, inversion, and full retrograde

quiz.prompt: In a fugue, a short melody called the subject is first stated alone in one voice, and then:
quiz.answer: Imitated in turn by each of the other voices
