quiz.explain: A fugue develops through imitation: the subject enters successively in additional voices, weaving contrapuntal texture.
choices: Answered at once by a completely new melody line
Imitated in turn by each of the other voices
Never heard again in the rest of the whole piece
Played once more only at the very last bar

quiz.prompt: In invertible counterpoint at the octave, an interval and the interval it becomes once the two voices swap places always add up to 9. A third in the original therefore sounds as which interval number after the swap?
quiz.explain: 9 - 3 = 6, so thirds become sixths and sixths become thirds. That rule is why composers favour thirds and sixths in invertible writing: both members of the pair are consonant, while a fifth would invert to a fourth.

quiz.prompt: A fugue subject climbs a fourth and then steps down a second. Later the composer brings it back falling a fourth and rising a second, with the rhythm untouched. The subject has been:
quiz.answer: inverted
choices: inverted
retrograde
in stretto
augmented
quiz.explain: Inversion turns every interval upside down while keeping its size and rhythm. Retrograde would run the subject backwards, augmentation would stretch its note values, and stretto would pile entries on top of each other.

quiz.prompt: A Classical sonata-form movement in C major sends its second theme into G major in the exposition. When that theme comes back in the recapitulation, a listener following the score should expect it:
quiz.answer: in the tonic, C major
choices: in the tonic, C major
in G major again, exactly as in the exposition
in C minor, darkening the return
in D major, a step higher than before
quiz.explain: Because the recapitulation resolves the key conflict the exposition opened. The drama of sonata form is tonal: the exposition leaves home, the development wanders, and the recapitulation brings the foreign material back into the tonic. A recapitulation that simply repeated the exposition would resolve nothing.

quiz.prompt: A movement runs to 96 bars of 4/4 and the conductor keeps a steady 120 quarter-note beats a minute. How many seconds does the movement last?
quiz.explain: 96 bars of 4 beats is 384 beats; at 120 beats a minute that is 3.2 minutes, or 192 seconds.

quiz.prompt: A student writes two voices that move from a perfect fifth to another perfect fifth, both rising by step. The tutor marks it as an error. Why?
quiz.answer: Parallel fifths fuse the two voices, so their independence is lost
choices: Parallel fifths fuse the two voices, so their independence is lost
A fifth is a dissonance and has to resolve downward
Two voices are not permitted to sound a perfect fifth at any point in the piece
Perfect fifths are permitted only on strong beats
quiz.explain: Counterpoint exists to keep lines distinct; parallel perfect consonances make the ear hear one thickened line instead of two.

quiz.prompt: A composer needs a passage that raises tension without introducing any new material. Which device does the job?
quiz.answer: A sequence, repeating the motif a step higher each time
choices: A sequence, repeating the motif a step higher each time
A full and emphatic cadence in the home key of the movement
A verbatim repeat of the exposition
A held silence lasting four bars
quiz.explain: A rising sequence reuses one idea while raising pitch and harmonic pressure, which is why it fills so many development sections.

quiz.prompt: A listener asks why so many Classical finales are rondos. Which answer is grounded in how the form actually behaves?
quiz.answer: Its returning theme gives repeated arrival, while the episodes stay light and varied
choices: Its returning theme gives repeated arrival, while the episodes stay light and varied
It is the shortest form a composer can choose
It stays in a single key from beginning to end, which listeners feel is right for an ending
It needs no development of its material at all
quiz.explain: The recurring refrain makes a finale feel conclusive and easy to follow after the weight of a sonata-form first movement.

nodes.title: World Arts & Music
nodes.goal: Traditions beyond the Western canon.

quiz.prompt: A researcher spends two years in a Ghanaian town, learning to play in a drumming ensemble, recording funerals and festivals, and asking players what each pattern is for. Her methods belong to:
quiz.answer: ethnomusicology
choices: ethnomusicology
historical musicology, which works from written scores
music therapy, which treats patients through sound
acoustics, which measures how sound behaves
quiz.explain: Which studies music as something people do within a culture. Ethnomusicology treats music as social practice, so its evidence is fieldwork: participation, recording and what players themselves say. A discipline working only from notation could not have asked the questions she asked.

quiz.prompt: Much traditional Islamic religious art avoids depicting human and animal figures. Which decorative style did artists develop instead to adorn mosques and manuscripts?
quiz.answer: Geometric patterns and flowing arabesques
quiz.explain: In response to a general avoidance of figural imagery in sacred contexts, Islamic art flourished in geometry, arabesque, and calligraphy.
choices: Geometric patterns and flowing arabesques
Stained-glass window scenes of the saints
Carved marble statues of the nude human body
Realistic portrait paintings of living rulers

quiz.prompt: In classical Chinese art, painting is deeply tied to another brush-based art that shares the same tools and prizes expressive, controlled strokes. That companion art is:
quiz.answer: Calligraphy
quiz.explain: Chinese painting and calligraphy use the same brush and ink and share an aesthetic of expressive line, making them closely linked traditions.
choices: Oil portraiture
Fresco
Mosaic
Calligraphy

quiz.prompt: A Japanese ukiyo-e print needs one key block carved for the black outlines, plus a separate block for each colour. For a print using five colours, how many blocks must the carver cut?
quiz.explain: One key block plus five colour blocks makes six. Each block is printed onto the same sheet in turn, which is why a busy print can demand a dozen carvings before a single copy exists.

quiz.prompt: The ukiyo-e carver cuts a small right-angled notch into the same corner of every block in a set, and the printer lays each sheet of damp paper against it. What does that notch achieve?
quiz.answer: Each colour lands on the last, so the outlines stay filled
choices: Each colour lands on the last, so the outlines stay filled
It marks which block should be printed first
It lets the printer lift the block without smudging
It stops the damp paper tearing as it is peeled away
quiz.explain: The notch is a registration mark, called kento. Without it the reds drift off the faces; with it, ten separate printings still line up to the width of a hair.

quiz.prompt: A Hindustani recital opens with several minutes of unmetred playing: single notes, slow slides between them, no drum at all. Then the tabla enters and a cycle begins. That opening section does the work of:
quiz.answer: unfolding the raga's notes and character before any cycle starts
choices: unfolding the raga's notes and character before any cycle starts
tuning the instruments in front of the listeners
announcing the tala so listeners can count along
playing a fixed introduction set down by a composer
quiz.explain: The alap presents the raga itself: which notes, approached how, with which phrases carrying weight. Rhythm is withheld precisely so that pitch and ornament have the listener's whole attention.

quiz.prompt: A gamelan ensemble tunes its paired bronze instruments slightly apart in pitch. A visiting pianist declares them out of tune. What is he missing?
quiz.answer: The deliberate beating between the pairs, which gives the ensemble its shimmer
choices: The deliberate beating between the pairs, which gives the ensemble its shimmer
That bronze cannot be tuned to any precise pitch
That the ensemble tunes itself to a Western piano before each performance begins
That the tuning has drifted in the tropical heat
quiz.explain: The ombak, or wave, is a designed acoustic effect: two nearly equal pitches beat together and the sound pulses.

quiz.prompt: A tala cycle of 16 beats is played at 120 beats a minute. How many complete cycles pass in 4 minutes?
quiz.explain: 4 minutes at 120 beats a minute is 480 beats, and 480 divided by 16 gives 30 cycles.

quiz.prompt: A West African drumming ensemble layers patterns of different lengths over a repeating bell pattern. A student transcribes everything into 4/4 and the feel vanishes. What has been lost?
quiz.answer: The cross-rhythms, whose different lengths line up only now and then
choices: The cross-rhythms, whose different lengths line up only now and then
The tempo, which is faster than 4/4 can carry
The melody, which no staff notation can record
The dynamics, which the drummers vary from one cycle of the bell to the next
quiz.explain: Forcing every part into one metre imposes a single downbeat, and the music's interest lies exactly in parts that do not share one.

quiz.prompt: A museum puts a Navajo sandpainting permanently on display under glass. Explain how that conflicts with the object's own terms.
quiz.answer: The sandpainting is made for a healing ceremony and is destroyed when the ceremony ends, so its meaning lies in the making and the ritual use rather than in a lasting object; preserving it forever removes the impermanence the practice itself requires.
quiz.explain: Conservation is not neutral: keeping an object can contradict the practice that produced it.

nodes.title: Advanced Aesthetics & Theory
nodes.goal: Contemporary theory and the meaning of art.

quiz.prompt: An advertisement shows a chronograph watch against a mountain summit, and readers take the pairing to promise hard-won accomplishment. In Saussure's terms, the signified here is:
quiz.answer: the idea of achievement
choices: the idea of achievement
the printed image of the watch
the reader who buys the magazine
the actual watch on sale in the shop
quiz.explain: The signifier is the perceptible form, the printed image; the signified is the concept it calls up. The physical watch in the shop is the referent, which Saussure deliberately keeps outside the pair.

quiz.prompt: Postmodern theory is especially known for its skepticism toward:
quiz.answer: Grand narratives that claim to explain everything
quiz.explain: Postmodernism, following Lyotard, is characterized by incredulity toward 'metanarratives,' the totalizing stories that claim universal explanatory power.
choices: The use of bright color in any modern painting
Grand narratives that claim to explain everything
The very existence of public galleries and museums
The idea that artworks can ever be bought and sold

quiz.prompt: A contemporary artist exhibits a written set of instructions rather than a finished object, insisting that the idea itself is the real artwork. This reflects the influence of:
quiz.answer: Conceptual art
quiz.explain: Conceptual art holds that the concept or idea takes precedence over the crafted material object, so instructions alone can constitute the work.
choices: Renaissance realism
Classical sculpture
Conceptual art
Impressionism

quiz.prompt: Saussure denies that a word resembles the thing it names. Explain where a sign's meaning comes from on his account.
quiz.answer: From its place in a system: the link between signifier and signified is arbitrary, so a sign means what it does through its differences from the other signs available, not through any resemblance.
quiz.explain: Nothing about the sound cat suits a cat; what fixes it is that it is not cap, not cot, not dog. Meaning as difference within a system is the hinge that structuralism turns on, and post-structuralism then pushes further.

quiz.prompt: Benjamin claims that mechanical reproduction withers the aura of a work. A student pins a poster of the Mona Lisa above her desk. Which feature of that poster carries his point?
quiz.answer: It arrives anywhere on demand, while the panel keeps its own place and history
choices: It arrives anywhere on demand, while the panel keeps its own place and history
It shows the picture at rather less than half its true size
It costs far less than a ticket to the Louvre
It reproduces the colours a shade too warmly
quiz.explain: Aura, for Benjamin, is the here and now of the work: its unique presence in one place, carrying its own history. Fidelity and cost are beside the point, which is why a perfect copy would still lack it.

quiz.prompt: Warhol's Brillo Boxes stand in a gallery beside photographs of near-identical cartons stacked in a stockroom. Danto asks what makes one a work and the other a carton. His answer points to:
quiz.answer: an interpretation, carried by a theory and a history
choices: an interpretation, carried by a theory and a history
the higher quality of the plywood Warhol used
the greater beauty of the gallery version
the price a collector will pay for the gallery version
quiz.explain: Danto's case turns on indiscernible objects: if the eye cannot separate them, whatever makes one art is not visible. He locates it in an atmosphere of theory and a knowledge of art's history.

quiz.prompt: A museum buys a performance work that exists only when the artist herself performs it. She dies, and the board asks what the museum now owns. Which account best fits the work?
quiz.answer: A score plus a lineage of authorised performers
choices: A score plus a lineage of authorised performers
A relic, since only the documentation now survives
Nothing at all, since the work ended with the artist
The copyright, which simply is the work
quiz.explain: Treating the piece as a performance type rather than a token object is what lets institutions keep such works alive at all.

quiz.prompt: A critic argues that a protest photograph circulating as a meme means something different from the identical file in an archive. Which theoretical claim is she leaning on?
quiz.answer: That meaning is produced in circulation and context, not fixed inside the image
choices: That meaning is produced in circulation and context, not fixed inside the image
That digital files degrade slightly with each copy
That archives are politically neutral holders of images
That the photographer's intention alone settles how the image ought to be read by anyone
quiz.explain: The pixels are identical, so any difference in meaning has to come from where the image is met and by whom.

quiz.prompt: An institution commissions a mural for a neighbourhood, and residents say it addresses the funders rather than them. Which critical framework names that problem most directly?
quiz.answer: Site-specificity, which asks whose place and whose public a work addresses
choices: Site-specificity, which asks whose place and whose public a work addresses
Formalism, which restricts attention to design decisions inside the frame itself
Aura, which concerns the presence of an original
Medium specificity, which ties an art to its material
quiz.explain: Site-specific critique treats the audience and the location as part of the work, so a mismatch between them is a fault in the work itself.

quiz.prompt: Barthes announces the death of the author. Explain what that move buys a reader, and what it costs.
quiz.answer: It frees the reader to build meaning from the text and its language rather than hunting for the writer's biography, which opens the work to plural readings; the cost is that historical context and the author's situated position lose their authority to constrain interpretation, so some readings become hard to rule out.
quiz.explain: The gain in interpretive freedom is paid for in interpretive discipline, which is why the essay is still argued over.

nodes.title: Mastery of a Craft
nodes.goal: What sustaining an original creative practice actually requires — a multiple-choice quiz can test understanding of this, not the work itself.

quiz.prompt: For a practicing artist, a portfolio primarily serves to:
quiz.answer: Show a curated body of work and one's direction
quiz.explain: A portfolio is a deliberately selected set of works that communicates an artist's abilities and creative identity to others.
choices: Show a curated body of work and one's direction
Store leftover paint, brushes and other supplies
List every piece ever made, with no real selection
Remove any need to keep making new work later

quiz.prompt: Which habit best supports developing sustained, original creative work over many years?
quiz.answer: Regular practice plus reflection and revision
quiz.explain: Mastery and original output grow from consistent, deliberate practice with reflection and revision, not from waiting passively for inspiration.
choices: Copying other artists' finished works exactly
Avoiding all feedback and outside criticism
Regular practice plus reflection and revision
Waiting for rare bursts of sudden inspiration

quiz.prompt: Psychologists commonly define creativity as producing work that is both:
quiz.answer: Novel and also valuable in its context
quiz.explain: The standard definition of creativity requires both novelty and value/appropriateness; mere novelty alone is not enough.
choices: Popular with crowds and instantly loved
Novel and also valuable in its context
Expensive to buy and physically large
Fast to make and very simple to copy

quiz.prompt: An artist has forty finished pieces and may send only twelve to a gallery. Explain why cutting down to twelve usually serves her better than sending everything.
quiz.answer: A portfolio is read as one thing, and the weakest pieces set the impression as much as the best do. Sending only her strongest work shows both the level she can reach and her own quality of judgement about which work is which.
quiz.explain: Selection is itself a demonstration of taste. A viewer who sees uneven work does not average it; they wonder whether the artist can tell the difference.

quiz.prompt: A pianist practises three hours a day by playing each piece straight through at full tempo, and her error rate in the same four bars has not shifted in a year. Her teacher says the hours are not the problem. What should change?
quiz.answer: Isolating those four bars, slowing them until they come out clean, then rebuilding speed
choices: Isolating those four bars, slowing them until they come out clean, then rebuilding speed
Learning more pieces, so the hands meet more patterns
Adding a fourth hour to the daily session
Performing the piece in public more often
quiz.explain: Deliberate practice targets the specific failure, at a speed where it can be corrected, with feedback each repetition. Playing through rehearses the error along with everything else.

quiz.prompt: A popular book claims that ten thousand hours of practice produce mastery in any field. A later meta-analysis of hundreds of studies found that accumulated practice accounted for a minority of the differences between performers in every domain it examined. Which conclusion follows?
quiz.answer: Practice counts, but not alone
choices: Practice counts, but not alone
Talent alone decides mastery
Practice explains almost nothing about performance
The ten thousand hour figure holds outside music
quiz.explain: A variable that explains part of the spread is neither the whole story nor nothing. Starting age, teaching, working memory and sheer opportunity take up much of the rest, and none of that makes practice optional.

quiz.prompt: A novelist's second book repeats the structure of her first, and reviewers call it safe. She sets herself a rule: no first-person narration. Why can an arbitrary constraint help?
quiz.answer: Removing a habitual option forces choices the habit had been hiding
choices: Removing a habitual option forces choices the habit had been hiding
Constraints raise output, and volume produces quality
Third-person narration is the more respected form
Reviewers reward formal experiment almost as a matter of course these days
quiz.explain: A constraint is a way of making the default visible; you cannot revise a choice you never noticed you were making.

quiz.prompt: A painter shows work in progress to a trusted peer halfway through rather than at the end. What is the trade-off?
quiz.answer: Correction while change is cheap, but a risk of losing direction
choices: Correction while change is cheap, but a risk of losing direction
A faster finish to the work, against the risk of imitating the peer's style
Better materials at a lower price, against a higher cost per finished work
A stronger portfolio, against fewer exhibitions
quiz.explain: Feedback is most actionable before the work sets, and most dangerous before the artist's own intention has firmed up.

quiz.prompt: A composer keeps every discarded sketch instead of deleting it. Give two ways that practice pays off.
quiz.answer: Material rejected for one piece often turns out to fit another later, so the sketches become a working resource; and the surviving record shows how a finished piece was arrived at, which makes the process examinable and repeatable rather than mysterious.
quiz.explain: Keeping the trail turns individual pieces into a body of work with a method behind it.

quiz.prompt: A dancer returns from injury and finds that her old daily routine now causes pain. Her teacher tells her to rebuild the practice rather than push through. Which principle is at work?
quiz.answer: A practice must fit the body that has it
choices: A practice must fit the body that has it
Ability declines with age, so expectations must be lowered
Rest by itself restores technique without any practice
Pain is a dependable sign that effort is productive
quiz.explain: Deliberate practice is adaptive by definition: the routine serves the goal and the body, not the other way round.

nodes.title: Art at the Frontier
nodes.goal: New media, generative and computational art.

quiz.prompt: Sol LeWitt's Wall Drawing #118 exists as an instruction: place fifty points at random on a wall, then connect every point to every other with straight lines. Two teams draw it in two cities and the walls plainly do not match. LeWitt calls both of them the work. Which account of the piece fits that claim?
quiz.answer: The instruction fixes the work, and each wall shows one outcome it permits
choices: The instruction fixes the work, and each wall shows one outcome it permits
The difference records a failure to follow the instruction
The first wall counts as the work and the second as a copy
The work exists in the photographs, not on either wall
quiz.explain: LeWitt separated the idea from its execution and let others draw it, so variation between installations is a property of the piece rather than a mistake in it. The same move underlies generative work made with code.

quiz.prompt: Two installations share a gallery. One projects a fixed ten-minute film of a forest on a loop. The other projects a forest that thins where visitors walk and closes behind them, driven by sensors in the floor. What does the second make of a visitor that the first cannot?
quiz.answer: A component of the work, since the image depends on where people go
choices: A component of the work, since the image depends on where people go
A better-informed viewer, since more of the forest gets shown
A critic of the work, since the sensors record what people do
A spectator at a longer film, since the loop never repeats
quiz.explain: Interactive work takes the audience as an input, so no two visits produce the same piece and the artist authors a range of behaviour rather than one fixed image. That is a different kind of authorship, not merely a different medium.

quiz.prompt: An artist writes computer code that uses randomness to draw thousands of unique flowing lines, then runs the program to create each new piece. This is best classified as:
quiz.answer: Generative art
quiz.explain: Using an autonomous coded system with randomness to produce the artwork is a defining case of generative art.
choices: Classical sculpture
Traditional oil painting
Documentary photography
Generative art

quiz.prompt: Wall Drawing #118 joins each of its fifty points to every other point with one straight line. How many lines does a finished drawing contain?
quiz.explain: Each of the 50 points joins the other 49, and that counts every line twice: 50 x 49 / 2 = 1,225. A one-sentence instruction specifies an object no one could hold in mind.

quiz.prompt: A studio trains a model on ten thousand scanned paintings, generates two thousand images overnight, and exhibits nine of them. A critic argues that crediting the model as the artist misdescribes what happened. Which fact about the process most supports the critic?
quiz.answer: People chose the training set and picked nine from two thousand
choices: People chose the training set and picked nine from two thousand
The model produced images unlike anything in the training set
The exhibited images sold for more than the studio expected
The model ran overnight with nobody watching it
quiz.explain: The critic's claim concerns where the decisions sat, so evidence about decisions counts and evidence about novelty, price or autonomy does not. Novelty in particular is compatible with either account.

quiz.prompt: An artist posts a video work as a free download that anyone may keep, and separately sells one signed certificate naming a single owner. A collector pays six figures for the certificate. Which claim does that arrangement put to the test?
quiz.answer: That scarcity, not access, carries the price
choices: That scarcity, not access, carries the price
That a work loses its meaning once it is copied
That collectors care most about an artist's technique
That digital files cannot be owned by anybody at all
quiz.explain: Everyone can watch the work; one person owns a document saying so. The experience and the ownership have been prised apart, which is exactly the split Benjamin predicted reproduction would force into the open.

quiz.prompt: A generative work is sold as a token pointing at code hosted on a single server. Five years on the server is gone and the image will not render. What does the collector hold?
quiz.answer: A pointer to something now absent
choices: A pointer to something now absent
The work itself, since the token simply is the artwork
Nothing, because generative art cannot be owned at all
A copy of the last rendered image, kept by default
quiz.explain: Conservation of software art is a preservation problem: the runtime, libraries and assets are as much the work as the token is.

quiz.prompt: An artist trains a model only on twenty years of her own drawings and exhibits the results. A critic who objects to models trained on scraped work finds one objection answered and another not. Which is which?
quiz.answer: Consent is answered; authorship is not
choices: Consent is answered; authorship is not
Both are answered, since she owns all of the training data
Neither is answered, since every model works the same way
Only the authorship question is answered by her method
quiz.explain: Sourcing and authorship are separable complaints, and settling one leaves the other exactly where it was.

quiz.prompt: A generative piece places 30 points and draws one straight line between every pair of points. How many lines does it draw?
quiz.explain: Each of 30 points joins 29 others and every line is counted twice, so 30 x 29 / 2 = 435.

quiz.prompt: An interactive installation logs each visitor's movement in order to shape the projection, and the gallery posts no notice. Which issue should the artist deal with first?
quiz.answer: Informed consent for the data the work collects
choices: Informed consent for the data the work collects
The frame rate of the projected image
Whether the source code is released openly
Who holds the copyright in the projected imagery
quiz.explain: Once an artwork becomes a sensing system, the ethics of collection apply to it exactly as they would to any other.
